findings.title: Blocklist lookup is case-sensitive, so a case variant of a blocked address gets through
findings.body: `should_block?` looks up `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` using the raw value. Nothing normalizes the address before the lookup: `User.new_from_params` assigns `params[:email]` as typed and `User` has no downcasing callback. An entry for `spammer@spamclub.com` therefore does not match a signup with `Spammer@SpamClub.com`, and the spammer can register anyway. The existing domain restrictions in the same validator use a case-insensitive regex, so they are not affected. The uniqueness validation on `BlockedEmail#email` is also case-sensitive, so case-variant duplicate entries can be created. Normalize with `Email.downcase` on both the stored value and the lookup input, or match case-insensitively.

findings.title: Validation has a side effect that inflates match_count on every valid? call
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` increments `match_count` and saves the record each time it runs. It runs on every validation of a changed email. `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` (line 168) and then `user.save` (line 172), which validates again, so one blocked signup attempt is counted twice. The statistic is wrong, and any other `valid?` call also inflates it. Record matches in an explicit step outside the validator, and keep the validator read-only.

findings.title: Whitelist regex is unanchored, so suffix-extended domains pass the whitelist
findings.body: The whitelist check builds `/@(gmail\.com)/i` with no end anchor. An address such as `attacker@gmail.com.evil.example` matches and passes a `gmail.com` whitelist. The code was carried over from `User#email_in_restriction_setting?`, but it now lives in a new validator and the whitelist is an access-control policy. Anchor the domain (for example `/@(domain)$/i` after escaping) and compare the domain part exactly. The domain strings are also interpolated into the regex without `Regexp.escape`.

findings.title: match_count is a non-atomic read-modify-write that loses concurrent increments
findings.body: `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save` reads the count, adds one in Ruby, and writes it back. Two concurrent signups matching the same entry can both write the same value, so the count is undercounted. The full `save` also re-runs validations, including a uniqueness query, for what is a counter bump. Use an atomic database update such as `BlockedEmail.update_counters` or `update_all` with `match_count = match_count + 1`.

findings.title: Client caches server email rejections for the session and never re-checks them
findings.body: Any server error on `email` pushes the address into `rejectedEmails`, which is a controller-lifetime array. Later the client treats that address as invalid without asking the server. If an admin later removes the block or changes the whitelist, the user is still blocked in the browser until a reload. The client also overrides the server's specific message with the generic `user.email.invalid` text. The server should stay the only authority on blocked addresses, so keep the rejection only for the current form submission or drop the client-side check.

findings.title: Specs stub out the blocklist lookup, so the real behavior is untested
findings.body: Both examples stub `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so the tests never touch the database or the normalization path. Nothing covers case variants of a blocked address, which is the bypass above. Nothing checks that a blocked signup through `User`/`UsersController` is rejected, or that a single attempt increments `match_count` only once, which is the double-count above. The uniqueness and case behavior of `BlockedEmail` are also untested. Add an integration-level spec that creates a blocked entry, attempts signup with a case-variant address, and asserts the rejection and the count.
